findings.recommendation: The character classes are ASCII-only, so the character right before `@` must be ASCII and the domain must be ASCII. `logInfo("signup", { email: "zoë@example.org" })` or an internationalised domain such as `jean@exämple.fr` matches nothing and the full address reaches the hosting provider's logs, kept 90 days (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), Art. 25), although the header promises the logger "never writes a full e-mail address". Match on the `@` with Unicode-aware classes (e.g. `[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+` with the `u` flag) and add a test with a non-ASCII local part and domain.
findings.title: Addresses with non-ASCII characters are logged in full

findings.recommendation: The pattern requires a literal `@`. A logged URL or query string such as `/reset?email=ada.lovelace%40example.org` is written unchanged, so the address lands in the logs in full. No caller logs URLs yet, hence the low confidence. Also match `%40` (case-insensitive) as the separator, or decode before masking, and cover it with a test.
findings.title: Percent-encoded addresses escape the mask

findings.recommendation: For a personal or small-company domain (`j***@janedoe.com`), the first letter plus the domain can be enough to re-identify the person, so the logs still hold personal data in pseudonymised form. Whether that is acceptable depends on the domains in real traffic, which the review could not see. If the domain is not needed for debugging, mask it too, or log a keyed hash of the address instead.
findings.title: Masked form keeps the first letter and the full domain

findings.recommendation: Only the values go through `maskEmails`. A caller that builds `fields` from a map keyed by address (e.g. `{ "ada@example.org": 3 }`) writes the address in full. No such caller exists yet. Mask the keys as well: `safe[maskEmails(key)] = …`.
findings.title: Field keys are written unmasked
